title: Lowest common ancestor by binary lifting
prompt: Given a tree on n nodes as a list of undirected edges, root it at node 0 and answer lowest-common-ancestor queries. NewLCA(n, edges) preprocesses it and Query(u, v) returns the deepest node that is an ancestor of both u and v (a node counts as its own ancestor). Query must be O(log n): the tests build a 200000-node path and run 400000 queries, so climbing one edge at a time is far too slow.
explanation: Two tables carry everything: depth[v] from one traversal of the tree, and up[k][v], the ancestor of v exactly 2^k edges above it, built from up[k][v] = up[k-1][up[k-1][v]]. That is O(n log n) to build. A query first lifts the deeper node by the bits of the depth difference, which lands both nodes on the same level; if they coincide, that node is the answer. Otherwise it walks k from high to low and lifts both nodes only when their 2^k ancestors differ, which keeps them strictly below the LCA the whole way, so after the loop their parent is the LCA. Building depths with a queue rather than recursion matters here: the test tree is a path 200000 deep.
hints: Two preprocessed tables are enough: how deep each node is, and where you land jumping a power of two upward.
Handle the depth gap first, using the binary representation of the difference.
For the second half, lift both nodes only when the jump keeps them below the answer, then look one step up.
refs: LC 236 Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
LC 1483 Kth Ancestor of a Tree Node

title: Strongly connected components
prompt: Given a directed graph on n nodes as a list of edges [from, to], return its strongly connected components: each group of nodes that can all reach each other. Return one slice per component; the order of the components and of the nodes inside each one does not matter. Every node belongs to exactly one component, so a node with no edges is a component of size one. This must be linear in nodes plus edges: the tests run 300000 nodes, so testing mutual reachability per node does not finish.
explanation: This is Kosaraju. First pass: a depth-first traversal of the graph that appends each node only after all of its out-neighbours are finished, producing an order by finish time. Second pass: take nodes in decreasing finish time and, from each unclaimed one, collect everything reachable in the reversed graph. That set is exactly one component, because reachability in the graph intersected with reachability in the reverse is mutual reachability, and the finish order guarantees you start at a node whose component sits at the top of the remaining condensation, so the reverse search cannot leak into a component that was already taken. Tarjan's single-pass lowlink algorithm is the other standard answer and is equally linear. Note the traversal here is an explicit stack with a per-node iterator index: recursion would be fine on paper but the test graph is 300000 nodes deep in the worst case.
hints: Mutual reachability means reachable forward and reachable backward, so keep the reversed adjacency too.
Order matters: the first pass exists only to decide which node to start the second pass from.
In the first pass, record a node after its out-neighbours are exhausted, not when you first see it.
refs: LC 1192 Critical Connections in a Network

title: A bounded worker pool that keeps order
prompt: Write parallelMap(items, workers, f) that applies f to every item and returns the results in input order, with at most workers calls to f running at any moment. workers below 1 counts as 1. The tests check all three properties: the results line up with the input, 16 items that sleep 40ms each finish in well under the sequential time on 8 workers, and the number of concurrent calls to f never exceeds the limit and does reach it.
explanation: Three separate requirements, each with its own mechanism. Bounding concurrency: start exactly workers goroutines, all ranging over one channel of jobs, so the number in flight can never exceed the number of goroutines no matter how many items arrive. Keeping order: send the index rather than the value and have the worker write out[i] directly, which is why no result channel and no sorting are needed. Knowing when to stop: close the jobs channel after the last send, which ends every worker's range loop, and Wait on the WaitGroup before returning. The slice writes need no mutex because each index is handed to exactly one worker and out is never reallocated, so no two goroutines touch the same memory. The alternative shape, one goroutine per item holding a buffered channel as a semaphore, is also correct and bounded, but it creates a goroutine per item, which is the wrong trade when items are numerous and f is cheap.
hints: The limit is easiest to enforce structurally: create exactly that many goroutines and feed them all from one channel.
Send the index, not the value, and the ordering problem disappears.
Two things end the run: closing the job channel stops the workers, and a WaitGroup tells you they are done.
refs: Go blog: Go Concurrency Patterns: Pipelines and cancellation
